questions.stem: Ecosystem services are best defined as:
options: the government programs that restore ecosystems damaged by development
the processes by which ecosystems recover after a natural disturbance
the benefits people obtain from ecosystems and their natural processes
the paid work done by rangers and scientists to manage protected areas
questions.explanation: Ecosystem services are the goods and benefits that ecosystems provide to people, such as food, clean water and climate regulation. Rangers and restoration programs are human services for ecosystems, not services from them.

questions.stem: Which of these is a renewable resource supplied by ecosystems?
options: Tin ore extracted from a granite deposit
Timber from a sustainably logged forest
Coal mined from an ancient swamp deposit
Natural gas drawn from an offshore field
questions.explanation: A renewable resource is replaced by natural processes within a human time scale if it is harvested no faster than it regrows, as timber can be. Coal, gas and metal ores form over millions of years, so they are non-renewable.

questions.stem: Coal is sometimes described as a resource provided by ecosystems even though it is non-renewable. Why?
options: It is continually produced by modern forests and swamps faster than it is mined
It is a mineral deposit made by volcanic activity, so it comes from the lithosphere
It forms quickly wherever peat is buried, so its supply is replaced within decades
It formed from plant matter made by photosynthesis in ancient swamp ecosystems
questions.explanation: Coal is the compressed remains of plants from swamp ecosystems that existed hundreds of millions of years ago, so it originated from ancient photosynthesis. It forms over geological time, far more slowly than it is used, which is why it is non-renewable.

questions.stem: Most of the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere has been produced by:
options: the breakdown of water vapour by lightning strikes
the release of gas from volcanoes and hot springs
photosynthesis by plants, algae and cyanobacteria
cellular respiration by animals and decomposers
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis splits water and releases oxygen as a by-product, and marine phytoplankton and cyanobacteria as well as land plants contribute. Respiration uses oxygen rather than producing it.

questions.stem: Why is ocean phytoplankton important to the oxygen supply that all organisms depend on?
options: Phytoplankton absorb oxygen from the air and store it in seawater for marine animals
Phytoplankton respire carbon dioxide and convert it directly into dissolved oxygen gas
Phytoplankton break down dead organisms in the deep ocean and release their oxygen
Phytoplankton photosynthesise across vast ocean areas, releasing much oxygen
questions.explanation: Phytoplankton are microscopic producers that carry out photosynthesis in the sunlit surface layer of the ocean, releasing oxygen. Organisms do not respire carbon dioxide; respiration consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: A forested catchment supplies a town's drinking water with little treatment. Which ecosystem process best explains why the water is clean?
options: Leaf litter releases chemicals that disinfect the water and kill every pathogen in streams
Shade from the canopy keeps water cold enough that bacteria and algae cannot survive in it
Vegetation and soil slow runoff, trap sediment and filter out nutrients
Forest trees take up most of the rainfall, so very little water reaches the streams at all
questions.explanation: Intact vegetation and soils intercept rain, slow overland flow, hold soil in place and filter sediment and nutrients, so streams stay clear. Forests do use water, but streams still flow; the benefit is the filtering, not stopping water from reaching them.

questions.stem: Wetlands are often described as the kidneys of the landscape. Which service does this describe?
options: Storing groundwater deep underground so that it can never be extracted by bores
Increasing the salinity of river water so that freshwater pests cannot survive
Trapping sediment and absorbing excess nutrients from water flowing through them
Producing most of the oxygen that is dissolved in the rivers flowing out of them
questions.explanation: Slow-moving water in wetlands drops its sediment, and wetland plants and microbes take up nitrogen and phosphorus, cleaning the water. This purification is why wetlands are compared with kidneys.

questions.stem: A council plans to drain a coastal wetland for housing. Engineers estimate that replacing its water-cleaning role would need a treatment plant costing millions of dollars. What does this comparison mainly show?
options: Treatment plants clean water more cheaply and reliably than any natural wetland can
Wetlands only provide value when people use them directly for fishing or recreation
Draining wetlands always improves water quality because stagnant water is removed
Ecosystem services have real economic value that is lost when ecosystems are cleared
questions.explanation: Costing a technological replacement puts a dollar figure on a service the wetland provides free, showing it has economic value. The comparison says nothing about the plant being cheaper; it shows the opposite, that losing the wetland adds a cost.

questions.stem: How do street trees and urban forests help provide clean air?
options: Their leaves trap fine particles and take up some gaseous pollutants
Their roots absorb sulfur dioxide from the air through the soil
Their bark releases ozone, which breaks down vehicle exhaust gases
Their flowers release oxygen that chemically neutralises smoke
questions.explanation: Leaf surfaces catch airborne particles and leaves take in gases such as nitrogen dioxide and ozone through their stomata. Trees do not neutralise smoke with oxygen, and releasing ozone near the ground would worsen air quality.

questions.stem: Which ecosystem process directly underpins the supply of fish caught in coastal waters?
options: Erosion of coastal cliffs that adds rock to the sea floor
Primary production by phytoplankton, seaweed and seagrass
Decomposition of plastic debris by marine bacteria
Evaporation of seawater that concentrates dissolved salts
questions.explanation: Fish are consumers, so the food web that supports them depends on producers capturing energy by photosynthesis. Without primary production there is no energy for higher trophic levels.

questions.stem: Native bees and other insects visit flowers in orchards next to bushland. Which ecosystem service do they provide for food production?
options: Decomposition of fallen fruit, which recycles nutrients
Pest control, by eating the caterpillars that damage leaves
Soil formation, by breaking down rock beneath the orchard
Pollination of crops, which increases fruit set and yield
questions.explanation: Pollinators transfer pollen between flowers, which many fruit and seed crops need to set fruit. Some insects do control pests or recycle nutrients, but visiting flowers is pollination.

questions.stem: Seagrass meadows in a shallow bay are lost after sediment and nutrient runoff increases. Fishers later report fewer juvenile fish of several species. The best explanation is that seagrass meadows:
options: warm the water enough for fish eggs to hatch in the winter
act as nursery habitat, giving young fish food and shelter
release oxygen that adult fish need to swim out of the bay
filter salt from seawater so juvenile fish avoid dehydration
questions.explanation: Seagrass beds provide shelter from predators and abundant food for juvenile fish and invertebrates, so they act as nurseries for fisheries. Seagrass does not remove salt from seawater, and fish are adapted to marine salinity.

questions.stem: Soil organisms, pollinators and natural predators of crop pests all support farming. Which statement best explains why clearing all native vegetation from a farm can reduce long-term food production?
options: It increases the area of crops, so more food is produced every year without any limit
It removes weeds that compete with crops, so yields always rise once clearing is done
It stops rain falling on the farm, because only native trees cause rainfall to occur
It removes habitat for organisms that pollinate crops, control pests and keep soil healthy
questions.explanation: Remnant vegetation shelters pollinators and predators of pests and protects soils from erosion, so losing it weakens services that farming depends on. Extra cropping area may raise output briefly but cannot increase it without limit.

questions.stem: Forests help regulate the global climate mainly by:
options: producing water vapour that destroys greenhouse gases
absorbing ozone, which is the main greenhouse gas
taking up carbon dioxide and storing carbon in wood and soil
releasing methane that reflects sunlight back into space
questions.explanation: Through photosynthesis, forests remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and store carbon in biomass and soils, acting as carbon sinks. Methane is itself a greenhouse gas and does not cool the planet.

questions.stem: Tasmania's tall wet eucalypt forests store very large amounts of carbon per hectare. If such a forest is cleared and burnt, what happens to its climate regulation role?
options: The carbon turns into oxygen as it burns, so atmospheric CO2 levels decrease
Stored carbon is released as carbon dioxide, and the forest stops absorbing more
Stored carbon is locked into the soil, so the climate is unaffected by clearing
Carbon dioxide uptake rises, because burnt land absorbs more CO2 than forest
questions.explanation: Burning oxidises the carbon in wood and litter to carbon dioxide, which enters the atmosphere, and cleared land no longer takes up carbon through the forest's growth. Clearing therefore turns a carbon sink into a carbon source.

questions.stem: Which ecosystem regulates local climate by cooling the surrounding area on hot days?
options: A paved plaza, through the storage of heat
A leafy park, through shade and transpiration
A large car park, through the reflection of heat
A bare paddock, through rapid soil evaporation
questions.explanation: Trees shade surfaces and cool the air as water evaporates from their leaves during transpiration. Paved surfaces store heat and release it later, which creates urban heat islands.

questions.stem: Saltmarshes and seagrass meadows take up carbon slowly but store it in waterlogged sediments for centuries. Why does draining a saltmarsh release carbon dioxide?
options: Saltmarsh plants respire faster once drained, but stop all photosynthesis instantly
Seawater releases dissolved carbon dioxide when it is replaced by fresh rainwater
Oxygen enters the dried sediment, so microbes decompose the stored organic matter
Draining lowers the temperature, so the sediment absorbs less carbon from the air
questions.explanation: Waterlogged sediments are low in oxygen, so decomposition is very slow and carbon accumulates. When drained, oxygen allows aerobic decomposers to break down the organic matter and release carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Which ecosystem service do coastal dunes held together by vegetation provide?
options: Supply of oxygen to the deep ocean through their plant roots
Protection of land behind them from storm waves and erosion
Production of most of the fresh water that flows into the sea
Regulation of ocean salinity by absorbing salt from sea spray
questions.explanation: Vegetated dunes absorb wave energy and act as a buffer and sand store during storms, protecting land and buildings behind them. Their roots bind the sand so the dunes are not eroded away.

questions.stem: Vegetation is cleared from steep slopes in a river catchment. Which loss of a protection service is most likely during heavy rain?
options: Lower runoff, so the downstream towns receive less water after storms
More rapid runoff, raising the risk of erosion, landslips and flooding
Less evaporation, so the river dries out completely during each storm
Higher groundwater salinity, so the river freezes in the colder months
questions.explanation: Plant cover and roots slow water, increase infiltration and bind soil, so clearing increases runoff speed and volume, erosion and flood peaks downstream. Clearing increases rather than decreases runoff.

questions.stem: Kelp forests and seagrass beds near a coastline are lost. Which change to the coastline is most likely?
options: Seawater becomes fresher, so beaches become more stable over time
Waves reach the shore with more energy, increasing coastal erosion
Waves reach the shore with less energy, increasing sand deposition
Tides become weaker, so less water reaches the intertidal zone
questions.explanation: Kelp and seagrass damp waves and help hold sediment, so losing them lets more wave energy reach the shore and increases erosion. Tides are driven by the Moon and Sun, not by marine vegetation.

questions.stem: A coastal town must choose between restoring mangrove and saltmarsh along an estuary or building a concrete sea wall. Which advantage does the ecosystem option offer that the sea wall does not?
options: It removes all flood risk permanently, because vegetation stops storm surges entirely
It costs nothing to establish, because plants never need planting or any maintenance
It protects the town immediately, because the vegetation reaches full size in weeks
It also provides habitat, filters water and stores carbon while reducing wave energy
questions.explanation: Restored coastal vegetation buffers waves while also delivering other services such as nursery habitat, water filtering and carbon storage. It reduces risk rather than removing it entirely, and it takes years to establish.

questions.stem: A reserve protects a large area of intact forest that is the catchment for a city's water supply. Which ecosystem services does this reserve mainly provide to the city?
options: Non-renewable resources such as coal, oil and metal ores from mines
Food production from cropping, and grazing land for beef cattle
Treatment of the city's sewage and industrial waste in its streams
Clean water, protection of soils from erosion, and carbon storage
questions.explanation: Forested catchments supply clean water, hold soils in place and store carbon. A protected catchment is not used for mining or farming, and streams should not be used to treat a city's waste.

questions.stem: An ecological footprint measures:
options: the mass of carbon dioxide released when a population burns fuel for electricity and for transport
the area of productive land and water needed to supply a population's resources and absorb its wastes
the total area of land a country controls, including its national parks and its territorial waters
the number of plant and animal species that have become extinct as a result of a population's activity
questions.explanation: An ecological footprint converts consumption and waste into the biologically productive area required to sustain them. Carbon dioxide emissions are one component, the carbon footprint, but not the whole footprint.

questions.stem: Which list contains factors that are included when calculating a person's ecological footprint?
options: Energy, food, housing, transport and waste
Height, age, income, education and health
Rainfall, soil type, altitude and latitude
Biodiversity, endemism, habitat and range
questions.explanation: Footprint calculators add up the land and water needed for the energy, food, housing, transport, goods and waste of a person or population. Personal traits and the physical features of a region are not footprint factors.

questions.stem: Ecological footprints are usually expressed in:
options: kilowatt hours per household
litres of water per household
global hectares per person
tonnes of rubbish per person
questions.explanation: A global hectare is a hectare of land or water with world-average biological productivity, which allows different land types and countries to be compared. Waste mass, energy and water use are inputs, not the unit of the footprint.

questions.stem: For a typical person in a high-income country, which component usually makes up the largest share of the ecological footprint?
options: The forest area needed to absorb CO2 from burning fossil fuels
The built-up land covered by the person's house, roads and workplace
The fishing grounds needed to supply the seafood that the person eats
The landfill area needed to bury the rubbish the person throws away
questions.explanation: The carbon component, the area needed to absorb emissions from energy use and transport, is usually the largest part of high-income footprints. Built-up land and landfill are real components but much smaller.

questions.stem: A family switches from driving to work to catching the bus and riding bicycles. Which part of its ecological footprint is most directly reduced?
options: Transport, through lower fossil fuel use
Housing, through a smaller building area
Food, through less land for crops grown
Waste, through fewer goods sent to landfill
questions.explanation: Driving burns petrol, so shifting to shared and active transport reduces the carbon from transport. The family's house, diet and rubbish are unchanged by how they travel.

questions.stem: Which household change would most reduce the food part of an ecological footprint?
options: Storing fresh vegetables in the freezer for months
Eating meals at the same table as the whole family
Eating less red meat and more plant-based protein
Buying food in larger packets less often each week
questions.explanation: Producing red meat needs much more land, feed and energy per kilogram than plant foods because energy is lost at each trophic level. Packet size and storage habits make little difference by comparison.

questions.stem: Two houses are the same size. One is well insulated, faces north and uses solar panels; the other is uninsulated and heated by electric heaters running on coal-fired power. Why does the first house have a smaller housing footprint?
options: It needs less energy for heating, and its electricity produces fewer emissions
It was built with more land around it, so the footprint is spread more widely
It is occupied for fewer hours, so the building uses fewer resources each year
It uses more electricity overall, which is always better than burning a fuel
questions.explanation: Insulation and north-facing design cut the energy needed for heating, and solar electricity produces far less carbon dioxide than coal-fired power. Both reduce the carbon component of the housing footprint.

questions.stem: Earth's biocapacity is about 1.6 global hectares per person. A country's average footprint is 4.8 global hectares per person. If everyone lived like this, how many Earths would be needed?
options: 3 Earths
1.6 Earths
4.8 Earths
7.7 Earths
questions.explanation: Divide the footprint by the biocapacity available per person: 4.8 / 1.6 = 3. Multiplying instead of dividing gives about 7.7, which is not the number of Earths.

questions.stem: A region has a biocapacity of 300 000 global hectares and a population of 50 000 with an average footprint of 9 global hectares per person. Which statement is correct?
options: Its footprint is 300 000 gha, so it is exactly within its own biocapacity
Its footprint is 450 000 gha, so it has an ecological reserve of 150 000 gha
Its footprint is 6 gha in total, so it uses far less than its biocapacity
Its footprint is 450 000 gha, so it has an ecological deficit of 150 000 gha
questions.explanation: Total footprint is 50 000 x 9 = 450 000 gha, which exceeds the biocapacity of 300 000 gha by 150 000 gha. A footprint larger than biocapacity is a deficit, not a reserve.

questions.stem: Average ecological footprints per person in high-income countries are several times larger than in low-income countries. Which factor best explains this?
options: Colder climates in every rich country, so more food has to be eaten
Higher consumption of energy, goods, meat and transport per person
Larger families, so each household needs more land to grow its food
Lower population density, so cities take up more space per person
questions.explanation: Footprints rise with consumption: wealthier populations use more energy, travel more, eat more meat and buy more goods. Not all high-income countries are cold, and household size is not the driver.

questions.stem: City A and City B have similar incomes and lifestyles, but City A's electricity comes almost entirely from hydro and wind power while City B's comes mainly from burning coal. Which difference in their footprints is most likely?
options: City A has a smaller carbon component, as its electricity emits far less CO2
City A has a larger carbon component, because hydro dams flood productive land
Both cities have the same footprint, because their electricity use is the same
City B has a smaller footprint, because coal releases its energy more efficiently
questions.explanation: The carbon component depends on the emissions from energy, so renewable electricity greatly reduces it even when consumption is the same. Dams do occupy land, but that area is small compared with the forest needed to absorb coal emissions.

questions.stem: A rural village grows most of its own food and uses little fuel, while a nearby city imports food and goods from around the world. Why is the city's footprint likely to fall mostly outside its own boundaries?
options: Cities are excluded from footprint calculations, so their imports count for other places
Its residents consume less than villagers, so the footprint must be shared with them
Imported food needs no land, so the city's footprint is counted only by its buildings
Land and energy used to produce and transport its imports are counted in its footprint
questions.explanation: A footprint is based on consumption wherever the resources come from, so the farmland, forests and fuel used to supply imports count towards the city. A city's own area is small, so most of the land it depends on lies elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine limitation of using ecological footprints to compare populations?
options: They do not capture every impact, such as toxic pollution or loss of biodiversity
They cannot be calculated for countries, only for individual people and families
They measure only water use, so they ignore energy, food, housing and transport
They give the same result for every country, so no comparisons can be made
questions.explanation: Footprints focus on the productive area needed for resources and carbon absorption, so impacts such as toxic chemicals, biodiversity loss and soil degradation are poorly captured. They are routinely calculated for countries and include energy, food, housing and transport.

questions.stem: A student's footprint calculator gives 7 global hectares. Which change would cut the waste part of the footprint most?
options: Using more single-use packaging to keep food fresh longer
Buying fewer new goods, and reusing and repairing items
Putting all household rubbish into one larger wheelie bin
Burning garden waste in the backyard instead of composting
questions.explanation: Reducing consumption and reusing items avoids both the resources used to make goods and the waste produced when they are thrown away. Burning garden waste releases carbon dioxide and smoke, and single-use packaging adds waste.

questions.stem: A government argues that its country's ecological footprint per person is only slightly above world biocapacity per person, so its population lives sustainably. Which response best evaluates this claim?
options: Footprints cannot be compared with biocapacity, because they use different units
Any footprint above biocapacity per person cannot be supported by Earth in the long term
The claim is correct, because a footprint only matters if it is ten times biocapacity
The claim is correct, because biocapacity per person rises whenever population grows
questions.explanation: If everyone had a footprint above biocapacity per person, humanity would use resources faster than ecosystems regenerate them, which is unsustainable. Biocapacity per person falls, not rises, as population grows, and both are measured in global hectares.
